title: The Borrowed Key

post.author: u/pomarine_valet_evaristo
post.title: I park cars at a riverside restaurant at night. At 02:41 our booking app read a guest's calendar. Our server never asked.

blocks.text: I'm Evaristo, night valet at Pomarine, a restaurant by the river. Guests hand me their keys all evening. If a car has a valet key, I ask for that one: it opens the door and starts the engine, but not the boot or the glovebox.

Pomarine's booking app lets guests sign in with Almanack, a calendar company, so the app can suggest table times around their diary. Letting one app use a narrow part of another account like this is called OAuth 2.0. A layer on top, OpenID Connect, also tells the app who signed in.
The app runs on our server, a computer that Lusotti, the studio that built it, rents for us. Lusotti set sign-in up the old way, in three steps.

Our page sends the guest to Almanack. She signs in there and says yes. Almanack sends her back with a token in the page address, the line at the top of the browser. A token is a long line of letters that works like my valet key: whoever holds it can read her calendar, for 30 days.
Every page also sends its address to an analytics tool, a service that counts our visitors. Its reports are shared with an outside marketing agency.

Last night Ms Quaranta, a regular, gave me her keys and showed me her phone. At 08:12 a text from a number she didn't know had listed her next three appointments, with times and places. Almanack's settings page lists every time an app read her calendar. Each line shows the date and time, which app, and where it came from.

25 Sep  20:16  Pomarine bookings  our server
14 Oct  02:41  Pomarine bookings  a computer not ours

blocks.label: her_calendar_reads_13_oct.png

diagram.aria: The night from 18:00 on 13 October to 10:00 on 14 October. Our server made no reads of Ms Quaranta's calendar all night. At 02:41 a read in Pomarine's name came from a computer that isn't Pomarine's. At 08:12 her text arrived.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from Almanack's page and our server's own log, 18:00 on 13 October to 10:00 on the 14th. Our server didn't touch her calendar all night. At 02:41 something reading as Pomarine did, from a computer that isn't ours. At 08:12 her text arrived.

blocks.text: Lusotti's developer, Otieno, searched the analytics reports. Her token, which his notes call token 3861, sits in a page address from 25 September, when she signed in at table 6. It had sat there 18 days, with 11 left to run.
Since 12 May, 4,300 sign-ins have each put a token in those reports. 860 came in the last 30 days, so 860 still work.
A token works for whoever holds it, the way my valet key works for anyone at the stand. Nothing in it says whose hand it should be in.
Almanack's record is true. Our app's key read her calendar. We didn't.

Almanack's guide offers a second way, the code flow. The page address carries only a one-time code, like the ticket I hand you for your car. Our server then swaps the code for the token by asking Almanack directly, so the token never passes through the browser.
The guide also adds PKCE, short for Proof Key for Code Exchange. At the start, our app makes up a secret for that one sign-in. Almanack swaps the code only for whoever shows that secret.
Mr Prendergast, the owner, wants a fix before Friday's bookings open. What should we change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Good picture, the valet key: it opens less than the full key, and it still works for anyone holding it. Before you choose, list every place a page address goes once it is in the browser, not only the analytics tool. Then look at what token 3861 was allowed to read, and for how long.

replies.author: u/pomarine_valet_evaristo
replies.text: Otieno says the page guests come back to, our return page, also loads a help-chat window run by another company, and it keeps the page address with every chat. 212 chats started on that page since May, 40 of them in the last 30 days. Ms Quaranta never opened it.

comments.author: u/strip_it_bressler
comments.text: The analytics tool is the bug, not the sign-in. Strip the page address from everything you send it, delete the old reports, and the old flow is fine: it ran five months without trouble. Rebuilding sign-in the week before Friday's bookings is how you break bookings.

comments.author: u/lusotti_dev_otieno
comments.text: Otieno from Lusotti. Our token asks Almanack for the full calendar: titles, places, guests. Which part of an account a token may read is called its scope. To suggest a table we only need free and busy times. I can narrow the scope tonight with one setting, no rebuild.

comments.author: u/pomarine_owner_prendergast
comments.text: Owner here. I never liked borrowing our guests' calendar keys. Let them sign in with a password of our own, kept by us, and there's no Almanack token to leak anywhere.

reply.prompt: Mr Prendergast wants a fix before Friday's bookings open. What should Pomarine change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Switch to the code flow with PKCE, so a token never appears in a page address.
options.part2: Otieno rebuilt sign-in by Thursday: the code flow with PKCE, and Almanack told to send guests back to one exact page. In the sim I switched the flow and replayed from 12 May: 4,300 sign-ins, 0 tokens in a page address, 0 in the analytics reports, 0 in the help-chat records. Each address carried a one-time code, spent once by our server and tied to that sign-in's secret. At 02:41 token 3861 was nowhere a stranger could copy it, and there was no read and no text. The real reports still held 860 working tokens, so Otieno asked Almanack to cancel every token it had given Pomarine, the agency lost access, and the old reports were deleted. Ms Quaranta signed in again on Saturday; her new token never left our server. Otieno's scope setting went in the week after.
options.senior: Fix where the token travels, not one place it landed. In the old flow the token rides in the page address, and an address goes to every script on the page, the browser's history and any tool that records it; stripping it from one tool leaves the rest. The code flow puts only a one-time code in the address and fetches the token server to server; PKCE ties that code to the sign-in that started it, so a copied code is worthless. RFC 9700 says not to use the old flow and to use PKCE. Then clean up what already leaked: cancel the tokens, cut the agency's access, delete the reports. Narrow the scope and shorten the lifetime too; they limit any future leak.

options.text: Strip page addresses from everything sent to analytics, and delete the old reports.
options.verdict: One door shut, the key still in the room
options.part2: Otieno stripped page addresses from analytics that night, and the agency deleted the old reports. In the sim I turned stripping on and replayed from 12 May: 0 tokens in the analytics reports, and at 02:41 token 3861 was not in any report to copy. But all 4,300 tokens still arrived in page addresses. The help chat kept 212 of them, and on the night 40 of those still worked. Every one also sat in its guest's browser history, on shared and family computers too, and would reach whatever outside script Lusotti adds to that page next. Bressler had found the place this token leaked, not the reason tokens leak.
options.senior: The analytics tool was where the token was found, not why it was exposed. A token in a page address is copied to every script the page loads, to browser history and to anything that records addresses; RFC 9700 warns that tokens "can end up in the browser's history of visited URLs" and says clients should not use the old flow at all. Stripping one tool is worth doing as clean-up, along with cancelling the tokens already out, but the lasting fix is a flow where the token never enters an address: the code flow with PKCE.

options.text: Ask Almanack for free and busy times only, not the full calendar with titles and places.
options.verdict: Right size key, same open counter
options.part2: Otieno narrowed the scope that night: new tokens may read free and busy times only. In the sim I set the scope to free and busy and replayed: at 02:41 token 3861 was still in the analytics reports, still had 11 days to run, and was still used from a computer that isn't ours. 860 working tokens still sat in the reports. The 08:12 text would have listed three busy times, no titles or places. Ms Quaranta said that was hardly better: a stranger would still know when she'd be out of the house.
options.senior: Narrow scopes are right, and RFC 9700 says a token's privileges should be restricted to what the app needs. Free and busy is all a table suggestion needs. But scope decides how much a leaked token shows, not whether it leaks. Busy times are still personal: they say when someone is away from home. Do it, alongside the real fix: stop the token travelling in page addresses with the code flow and PKCE, cancel the tokens already out, and shorten their lifetime.

options.text: Have guests sign in with a password of our own instead of borrowing an Almanack token.
options.verdict: No key to lose, and no calendar
options.part2: Lusotti built passwords of our own by December. In the sim I chose our own passwords and replayed: no Almanack tokens anywhere, and no table times from anyone's diary either. 2,900 guests now need a Pomarine password, and Pomarine has to store them: a slow hash with a salt for each, a check against common passwords, a second proof for new phones, everything in Who Are You. And the real analytics reports still held 860 working tokens until someone cancelled them.
options.senior: Dropping the borrowed key drops the feature the guests came for, and takes on a password store, which is a harder job than holding a narrow, short-lived token well. OAuth exists so an app never sees the other account's password. The flaw was where the token travelled, not that one was borrowed. Keep the sign-in, move to the code flow with PKCE, narrow the scope and shorten the lifetime, and cancel the tokens already leaked.

sim.title: Replay Pomarine's sign-ins, 25 September to 14 October
sim.lede: You're Evaristo at 20:00 on 25 September, just before Ms Quaranta signs in at table 6. The figures are given data: 4,300 sign-ins from 2,900 guests between 12 May and 13 October, each handing the app a new token; 860 of them in the 30 days before 02:41 on 14 October, and none in the hour before it; 212 help-chat chats started on the page guests come back to, 40 of them in those 30 days (she never opened one); 38 pages on our site whose address starts the same way. Choose the flow (the old token-in-address way, the code flow, the code flow with PKCE, or a password of our own), how long a token lasts (30 days, or one hour), the scope (full calendar, or free and busy), whether page addresses are stripped before they go to analytics, and which return pages Almanack accepts (any of our 38 pages, or one exact page). The lab counts where tokens went and whether one still worked at 02:41. Tokens are labels such as token 3861, never real ones.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run to 23:00 on 14 October as found: 4,300 tokens in page addresses and in the analytics reports, 860 still working, and at 02:41 token 3861 reads her full calendar. Switch to the code flow with PKCE: 0 tokens in any address, and no read. Go back and strip analytics instead: the reports hold 0, but 4,300 still travel in addresses and the help chat holds 40 that work. Try free and busy: the read still happens, showing busy times. Try one-hour tokens and our own passwords too.

explain.oneLine: Nothing was broken into. Pomarine used an old sign-in flow that handed each guest's calendar token back in the page address, and the page sent its address to an analytics tool whose reports an outside agency could read. Ms Quaranta's token sat there 18 days with 11 left to run, and whoever copied it read her calendar at 02:41 as Pomarine. The fix is the code flow with PKCE, so the token never enters an address, plus narrow scopes, exact return pages and short lifetimes.

steps.title: OAuth 2.0 lends a narrow key; OpenID Connect says who signed in.
steps.text: OAuth 2.0 lets one app use part of another account without ever seeing its password, the way a valet key starts the car without opening the boot. What the key may do is its scope. OpenID Connect adds one more thing: an ID token, a signed note from Almanack saying which person just signed in, so "Sign in with Almanack" can be a real sign-in, not just a borrowed key. Pomarine used both: the ID token to know the guest, the token to read her calendar.

steps.title: The old flow, step by step, and where the token sat.
steps.text: First, our page sent the guest to Almanack. Second, she signed in at Almanack and said yes to Pomarine reading her calendar. Third, Almanack sent her back to our return page with the token inside the page address; RFC 9700 calls this the implicit grant. Fourth, our page's own scripts read that address: the analytics tool copied it into reports an outside agency could read, and the help chat kept it with every chat. The browser also kept it in its history. What went wrong is the third step: once a token is in an address, every place that address goes gets a working key. 4,300 tokens took that path; 860 were still working on the night.

steps.title: The code flow with PKCE, step by step.
steps.text: First, our app makes up a fresh secret for this one sign-in, the code verifier, and sends the guest to Almanack with a locked form of it, the code challenge. Second, she signs in and says yes. Third, Almanack sends her back with a one-time code in the address, not a token. Fourth, our server sends that code and the secret to Almanack directly, server to server; Almanack checks the secret matches the locked form and hands over the token, and the code is spent. A code copied from the address on the way is worthless: it works once, and only with a secret that never left our app. The token itself never touches the browser.

steps.title: Exact return pages and narrow scopes.
steps.text: Almanack only sends guests back to return pages Pomarine registered. Lusotti registered a start of an address, so any of our 38 pages whose address began that way was accepted, including pages that load outside scripts. RFC 9700 says to match the return address exactly, character for character, so a code can only land on the one page built to receive it. Scope limits the damage when something does leak: free and busy times would have shown a stranger when Ms Quaranta was out, but not where or with whom.

steps.title: Short lifetimes, and the tokens already out.
steps.text: How long a token works is its lifetime. Almanack's tokens lasted 30 days, which is why a token copied on 25 September still worked on 14 October. A lifetime of an hour would have left 0 of the 860 working at 02:41. A short lifetime means the app needs a way to get a new token without asking the guest again, which the next case, Tokens, takes up. Changing the flow protects every future sign-in, but not the tokens already copied: ask the provider to cancel them, remove the agency's access, and delete the old reports.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the next sign-in. The guest's browser signs in at Almanack, which accepts one exact return page. Almanack sends a one-time code back through the address to our server, which keeps this sign-in's secret. Our server sends the code and the secret to Almanack's code swap; if the secret matches, Almanack hands over a token, server to server, and only our server uses it to read her free and busy times.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next sign-in. The address carries only a one-time code, and Almanack sends it only to one exact return page. Our server swaps the code, with this sign-in's secret, for a token that never touches the browser, and the token may read free and busy times only. Replayed from 12 May, 0 of 4,300 tokens enter a page address, and at 02:41 there is nothing to copy.

fix.title: The fix: the code flow with PKCE, then clean up what leaked
fix.text: Move sign-in to the authorization code flow with PKCE: a fresh secret for every sign-in, a one-time code in the address, and the token fetched server to server. Register one exact return page with Almanack instead of a start of an address. Ask for free and busy times only, and for the shortest token lifetime the feature can live with. Then deal with the 860 tokens still working: ask Almanack to cancel every token issued to Pomarine, remove the agency's access to the reports, delete the old reports, and tell the guests affected. Strip page addresses from analytics too, as general tidiness. In the sim, the code flow with PKCE puts 0 of 4,300 tokens in an address, and the 02:41 read never happens.

limits: PKCE protects the trip, not the token once it arrives. A token stored carelessly on our server, or written into our own logs, leaks just the same.
Changing the flow does nothing for tokens already copied. The 860 working tokens stay working until Almanack cancels them or they run out.
Short lifetimes mean the app must get new tokens without asking the guest each time, which brings its own key to guard; Tokens covers how long keys should live and how to cancel them.

head: What we change
Good
Bad
rows: 0 of 4,300 tokens in an address. A copied code is worthless. RFC 9700's advice.
A rebuild before Friday. The 860 tokens already out still need cancelling.
Strip addresses from analytics, delete old reports
One evening's work. The reports hold 0 tokens.
4,300 tokens still travel in addresses; the help chat holds 40 working ones; browser history keeps them all.
A leaked token shows less. One setting, no rebuild.
The 02:41 read still happens. 860 working tokens still in the reports. Busy times still say when she's out.
No table suggestions. 2,900 passwords to store and protect, with everything Who Are You warns about.

explain.seniorTake: A token is a key that works for whoever holds it, so the design question is where it travels. Keep it out of anything that gets copied: page addresses, browser history, analytics, logs. That is the whole case for the authorization code flow with PKCE: the front door, the browser, only ever carries a one-time code that is useless without a secret the app kept back, and the token moves server to server. Then shrink the damage of the leak you didn't foresee: exact return pages, the narrowest scope that serves the feature, and a lifetime measured in minutes or hours, not weeks. When a leak is found, the fix to the flow protects tomorrow; cancelling the tokens already out protects tonight. Do both, and treat any tool that records full addresses as a place secrets can end up.

realWorld.title: RFC 9700: don't use the implicit grant
realWorld.text: The OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice, January 2025, section 2.1.2: "clients SHOULD NOT use the implicit grant (response type `token`)", because such flows "are vulnerable to access token leakage and access token replay".

realWorld.title: RFC 9700: addresses end up in history
realWorld.text: Section 4.3: "Authorization codes and access tokens can end up in the browser's history of visited URLs". Section 4.3.2: "Clients MUST NOT pass access tokens in a URI query parameter".

realWorld.title: RFC 9700: PKCE, for every kind of app
realWorld.text: Section 2.1.1: "Public clients MUST use PKCE [RFC7636] to this end"; for confidential clients "the use of PKCE [RFC7636] is RECOMMENDED"; "Authorization servers MUST support PKCE". The advice "applies to all kinds of OAuth clients, including web applications".

realWorld.title: RFC 9700: exact return addresses, narrow tokens
realWorld.text: Section 2.1: "authorization servers MUST utilize exact string matching" when comparing return addresses. Section 2.3: "The privileges associated with an access token SHOULD be restricted" to what the app needs.

realWorld.title: RFC 7636: what PKCE is
realWorld.text: September 2015. "OAuth 2.0 public clients utilizing the Authorization Code Grant are susceptible to the authorization code interception attack." The fix "utilizes a dynamically created cryptographically random key called "code verifier"", and "A unique code verifier is created for every authorization request".

realWorld.title: OpenID Connect Core 1.0: who signed in
realWorld.text: "OpenID Connect 1.0 is a simple identity layer on top of the OAuth 2.0 protocol." Its main addition is the ID Token: "The primary extension that OpenID Connect makes to OAuth 2.0 to enable End-Users to be Authenticated is the ID Token data structure."

asked: Walk me through the authorization code flow with PKCE.
What does OpenID Connect add to OAuth?
Why should tokens never go in URLs?
interview.answer: OAuth 2.0 lets an app act on part of someone's account at another service without seeing their password: the user approves, and the app gets an access token limited by scope and lifetime. OpenID Connect sits on top and adds an ID token, a signed statement of who the user is, so the same exchange can be a sign-in. The authorization code flow with PKCE runs like this. The app makes a fresh random secret, the code verifier, and sends the user to the provider with a transformed form of it, the code challenge, plus an exact, registered return address. The user signs in and consents. The provider redirects back with a one-time authorization code, not a token. The app's server sends the code and the verifier to the provider's token endpoint; the provider checks the verifier matches the challenge and returns the tokens, server to server. A code intercepted on the way is useless without the verifier, and it works once. Tokens should never go in URLs because URLs are copied everywhere: browser history, analytics and error tools, other scripts on the page, logs. RFC 9700 says not to use the implicit grant, which returned tokens in the address, to use PKCE for every client, and to match redirect addresses exactly. A story I'd tell: a restaurant's booking app used the old flow, its analytics reports held 4,300 calendar tokens, 860 still live, and one was used to read a guest's calendar at 02:41. Stripping analytics would have closed one leak; the code flow with PKCE closes the path, and cancelling the leaked tokens deals with the ones already out.

terms.def: The riverside restaurant in this story, with a valet stand at the door and a booking app that lets guests sign in with Almanack.
The fictional calendar company in this story. Its tokens last 30 days, and its settings page lists every time an app read your calendar.
The fictional studio that built Pomarine's booking app and runs it on a server it rents for the restaurant.
A car key that opens the door and starts the engine but not the boot or the glovebox. This case's everyday picture of a narrow token.
A computer that runs a program for others over the internet. Pomarine's booking app runs on one.
A standard way to let one app use a narrow part of another account, with the owner's yes, without ever seeing that account's password. The app is handed a token instead.
A layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that also tells the app who signed in, using an ID token. It is what makes "Sign in with" a real sign-in.
OpenID Connect's signed note from the provider saying which person just signed in, and when.
A long string that works like a borrowed key: whoever holds it can do what it allows, such as reading a calendar, until it runs out. Also called an access token.
The line at the top of the browser showing where you are, also called a URL. Scripts on the page can read it, and the browser keeps it in its history.
Short for uniform resource locator: a page address.
A service that counts a website's visitors and the pages they see, usually by having the page send it the page address.
A chat window on a web page, run by another company, that keeps the page address with every chat.
A small program a web page loads and runs in the browser, such as an analytics tool or a help chat. It can read the page address.
The browser's own list of every page address visited, kept on the computer, including shared and family ones.
The old OAuth flow that hands the token straight back in the page address. RFC 9700 says apps should not use it.
Short for the authorization code flow: the address carries only a one-time code, and the app's server swaps it for the token directly with the provider.
What the code flow puts in the page address instead of a token. It works once, and only to be swapped for a token. Also called an authorization code.
Sent directly between two servers, never through the guest's browser or a page address.
Short for Proof Key for Code Exchange, said "pixy". The app makes up a secret for each sign-in, and the provider swaps the code only for whoever shows it.
PKCE's secret: a fresh random value the app makes for one sign-in and keeps back until it swaps the code.
A locked form of the code verifier that the app sends at the start. The provider later checks the verifier matches it.
Which part of an account a token may use, such as the full calendar or only free and busy times.
A narrow calendar scope: only when you are busy, with no titles, places or guests.
How long a token keeps working after it is issued. Almanack's were 30 days.
The page the provider sends the guest back to after sign-in, registered by the app in advance. Also called the redirect address or redirect URI.
The provider sends guests back only to a return page that matches the registered one character for character. RFC 9700 requires it.
Accepting any return page whose address starts the same way as the registered one. Pomarine's let 38 pages through.
Asking the provider to stop a token working before it runs out. Also called revoking it.
An app that cannot keep a secret of its own, such as one running wholly in a browser or on a phone. RFC 9700 says it must use PKCE.
An app with a server that can keep its own secret. RFC 9700 still recommends PKCE for it.
The company whose account an app borrows a key to, such as Almanack. It asks the person for a yes and hands out the tokens.
A password an app's own server uses to prove to the provider which app it is. It only stays secret on a server, never inside an app on people's phones.
The provider's address where an app's server swaps a one-time code for tokens, server to server.
When a site sends your browser on to another address, such as Almanack sending a guest back to Pomarine's return page.
Request for Comments: the numbered documents that define internet standards and advice.
The OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice, January 2025: today's advice on using OAuth safely.
The 2015 standard that defines PKCE.
Information about a person who can be identified, such as a guest's appointments.
An international standard for running information security. Annex A control A.8.5 covers secure authentication.
An audit report, written by an outside checker, on a company's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. CC6.1 covers logical access security.
The EU's General Data Protection Regulation. Article 32 asks for security suited to the risk of the personal data you hold.
Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act. Its protection obligation asks organisations to make reasonable security arrangements for personal data.

atWork: Search your own analytics, error-reporting and log exports for anything that looks like a token in a page address. It is a common pattern to find working access tokens sitting in an analytics export or a log file, copied there because a sign-in flow put them in the URL. Check four things. Does every "Sign in with" use the authorization code flow with PKCE, with no implicit grant left anywhere? Is each return address registered exactly, not as a start of an address? Does each token ask for the narrowest scope the feature needs, and how long does it live? And who outside your company can read your analytics and logs? If you find tokens, cancel them with the provider first, then fix the flow, then delete the copies. Build Night N5 in Nightwatch (teams, roles, API keys and an audit log; it unlocks after Who Are You, What May You Do, this case, Tokens, The Tenant Upstairs and The Watchman's Book) asks you to hand out keys that are hashed when stored and shown once; keep them out of URLs and logs the same way. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.8.5 (secure authentication) expects this; if SOC 2, criterion CC6.1 covers logical access security. If you hold EU residents' calendar data, GDPR Article 32 asks for security suited to the risk; if Singapore residents', the PDPA's protection obligation does. Build it in now, with a dated record of the flow, scopes and lifetimes, not at audit time.

recall.prompt: A fitness app adds "Sign in with" a large email provider so it can read a member's contacts and suggest friends. A developer notices the provider hands the access token back inside the page address, and the app's error-reporting tool records full page addresses. The team lead says: "Just hide addresses in the error reports." What do you tell her, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: A token in a page address reaches many places besides one tool: browser history, every script on the page, other logs
Use the authorization code flow with PKCE, so only a one-time code travels in the address and the token is fetched server to server
Treat the tokens already recorded as leaked: cancel them, and limit future damage with narrow scopes and short lifetimes

recall.model: Hiding addresses in one tool only closes one leak. A token in a page address also lands in browser history, reaches every script on the page, and turns up in other logs and analytics. Switch to the authorization code flow with PKCE: the address carries only a one-time code, tied to a secret the app made for that sign-in, and the app's server swaps it for the token server to server, so the token never enters an address. Then treat the tokens already recorded as leaked: revoke them with the provider and delete the reports. Ask for the narrowest scope that suggests friends, and keep tokens short-lived, so the next leak you didn't foresee shows less for less time.

recall.prompt: In the code flow with PKCE, what makes a one-time code copied from the page address worthless?
options: The code is encrypted so only the browser can read it
The provider swaps it only for whoever shows the secret the app made for that sign-in, and only once
The analytics tool strips codes from page addresses
The code only lets the holder read free and busy times
recall.why: PKCE ties each code to a fresh code verifier the app keeps back. The provider checks the verifier against the code challenge sent at the start, and the code works once. RFC 7636: a unique code verifier is created for every authorization request.

recall.prompt: What does OpenID Connect add to OAuth 2.0?
options: A way to encrypt the access token
An ID token saying who signed in, so the exchange can be a real sign-in
recall.why: OAuth 2.0 lends an app a key to part of an account; it doesn't say who the person is. OpenID Connect Core: "a simple identity layer on top of the OAuth 2.0 protocol", whose main addition is the ID Token.

recall.prompt: Pomarine had registered its return page as any address starting with its site's address, letting 38 pages through. What does RFC 9700 ask for instead?
options: Exact string matching against the one registered return page
Matching only the first part of the address
No return page; the guest goes back to the home page
recall.why: "Authorization servers MUST utilize exact string matching." With exact matching a code can only land on the one page built to receive it, not on any page that loads outside scripts.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Website sign-in has used the new flow since October, and the analytics reports have held no tokens since. In March Lusotti shipped a phone app for Pomarine. Its sign-in uses the code flow, but Otieno left out the extra step the website uses; instead he built Almanack's app password, its client secret, into the phone app itself, "so only our app can swap a code". The phone app has been downloaded 1,150 times.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What is wrong with the phone app's sign-in, and what should Lusotti do?

keyIdeas.idea: A secret built into an app on guests' phones is not secret: anyone with the app can dig it out, so the phone app is a public client
Use PKCE on every sign-in: a fresh secret made for each sign-in, never shipped inside the app
Treat the built-in secret as leaked: replace it with Almanack and take it out of the app

coldCase.model: A secret built into an app that sits on 1,150 phones is not a secret: anyone with the app can dig it out of every copy, so a phone app is a public client and can't keep a secret. It gives no protection to the code swap. Use PKCE on every sign-in instead: the app makes a fresh secret for each sign-in, the code verifier, sends its locked form at the start, and shows it when swapping the code, so a copied code is useless and nothing long-lived ships in the app. RFC 9700 says public clients must use PKCE. Then treat the built-in secret as leaked: ask Almanack to revoke it and issue a new client secret only for the website's server, and take it out of the phone app in the next release.
